questions.question: Never before ___ such a beautiful sunset.
questions.learningObjective: Invert subject and verb after a negative adverb
questions.explanation: When a sentence starts with a negative word like 'Never', the helping verb comes before the subject: 'had I seen'.
misconceptions: Forgot to swap the subject and helping verb
Used standard simple past without inversion
questions.curriculumReason: It has been a long time since you practiced inverted sentences.

questions.question: Rarely ___ so late to an important meeting.
questions.learningObjective: Invert subject and verb after rarely
questions.explanation: Sentences starting with 'Rarely' need question word order. So 'he arrives' becomes 'does he arrive'.
misconceptions: Used regular sentence order after a negative word
Inverted the main verb instead of using the helper 'does'
Used emphatic structure but failed to invert
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing advanced sentence structures.

questions.question: Not only ___ the cake, but he also ate the cookies.
questions.learningObjective: Invert subject and verb after not only
questions.explanation: Starting with 'Not only' triggers inversion, meaning you place 'did' before the subject.
misconceptions: Forgot to invert the subject and verb
Swapped the main verb instead of using a helper verb
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing advanced sentence structures.

questions.question: Were we to leave now, we ___ catch the next train.
questions.learningObjective: Match modals properly in hypothetical conditionals
questions.explanation: Because 'Were we to leave' sets up an imaginary situation, you need an imaginary result word like 'would' or 'could'.
misconceptions: Used a real-world possibility word instead of an imaginary one
Used a first conditional word in a second conditional sentence
Used present tense in a hypothetical sentence
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing hypotheticals to fix a recent error with 'will'.

questions.question: The restaurant is famous ___ its excellent seafood.
questions.learningObjective: Use for with famous
questions.explanation: In English, we say someone or something is 'famous for' a reason.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing which prepositions match specific adjectives.

questions.question: To 'beat around the bush' means to:
questions.learningObjective: Understand the idiom 'beat around the bush'
questions.explanation: When you 'beat around the bush', you talk about other things to avoid saying what is really important.
questions.curriculumReason: Expanding your knowledge of social idioms.

questions.question: If a movie is described as 'terrifying', it is:
questions.learningObjective: Understand the intense adjective terrifying
questions.explanation: Terrifying is a very strong word meaning extremely scary.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing intense adjectives to make sure they are fully mastered.

questions.question: Each of the students ___ given a textbook yesterday.
questions.learningObjective: Use singular verbs with each
questions.explanation: Words like 'each' and 'everyone' take singular verbs. Since this happened yesterday, we use 'was'.
misconceptions: Chose plural past instead of singular past
Chose plural present instead of singular past
Chose singular present instead of singular past
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing singular verb rules for groups of people.

questions.question: Which word is the closest in meaning to 'melancholy'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify a synonym for melancholy
questions.explanation: Melancholy means feeling a deep, quiet sadness.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing tricky adjective synonyms you struggled with.

questions.question: What is the best antonym for 'industrious'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify the antonym of industrious
questions.explanation: Industrious means very hardworking, so the exact opposite is lazy.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing advanced personality words.

feedback.headline: Great accuracy, but keep an eye on the clock!
strengths: You did a great job matching synonyms like 'thorough' and 'commence'.
Your spelling for tricky words like 'receive' was perfect.
weaknesses: You mixed up some extreme adjectives, like mistaking 'exhausted' for 'excited'.
You had some trouble with health idioms like being 'under the weather'.
feedback.advice: A lot of questions ran out of time on that round. Remember, a missed question just means time expired before you threw a punch! Try moving your gloves into the correct lane as soon as you know the answer, and wait for the target to arrive. We will practice the vocabulary you missed so you can react faster next time.

curriculum.title: Vocabulary Building & Quick Moves
curriculum.rationale: This session targets extreme adjectives and agreement words to clear up recent mix-ups. We also bring back some everyday idioms and grammar topics to build your reaction speed.

targetConcepts.reason: You recently confused words like 'unanimous' with 'kept secret' or 'decided quickly'. Let's master these agreement words.
You guessed 'very excited' instead of 'very tired'. We will practice extreme adjectives so you know exactly what they mean.
You saw a phrase about feeling slightly ill but chose 'very busy'. Let's review common health idioms.
It has been a little while since you practiced the past passive voice, so it is due for a review.
We will look at some phrases native speakers use all the time when chatting.

curriculum.sessionStrategy: Start with easy opposites and present-tense verbs to warm up. Then introduce medium and hard vocabulary drills to fix the mixed-up agreement and intensity words. This will build confidence and help speed up your reaction time.

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'huge'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify the antonym for huge
questions.explanation: Huge means very large, so the opposite is tiny, which means very small.
misconceptions: Loud relates to sound, not size.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing missed antonym concepts.

questions.question: Every weekend, we ___ tennis.
questions.learningObjective: Use base verb for first person plural routines
questions.explanation: For habits with 'we', use the base verb 'play' without an 's'.
misconceptions: Needs an 'are' before 'playing' for continuous actions.
The sentence is about a current weekly routine, not just the past.
questions.curriculumReason: Due for review; practicing present simple routines.

questions.question: I need to ___ this book to the library.
questions.learningObjective: Use vocabulary related to libraries
questions.explanation: When you finish a library book, you bring it back, which means to return it.
misconceptions: You borrow library books, you don't buy them.
Stealing is definitely not what you do at a library!
You read the book, but you have to give it back (return it) eventually.
questions.curriculumReason: Spaced review of everyday library vocabulary.

questions.question: Which phrase is the best greeting to say at 8:00 AM?
questions.learningObjective: Select the correct greeting for the morning
questions.explanation: 8:00 AM is early in the day, so we say 'Good morning'.
misconceptions: Evening is a greeting for the end of the day.
Afternoon is a greeting for after 12:00 PM.
Night is usually said right before sleeping.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing a basic concept missed in the previous round.

questions.question: I ___ very happy today.
questions.learningObjective: Conjugate the verb 'to be' for first person singular
questions.explanation: When talking about yourself right now, 'I' always pairs with 'am'.
misconceptions: Use 'is' with he, she, or it.
Use 'are' with you, we, or they.
The verb 'be' needs to change its form to match 'I'.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing present tense 'be' to build speed.

questions.question: If someone tells you they are 'starving', they are:
questions.learningObjective: Identify meaning of intensity adjectives
questions.explanation: Starving is a strong word that means you are extremely hungry.
misconceptions: Tired means you need sleep, often described as 'exhausted'.
Angry means you are mad, often described as 'furious'.
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting extreme adjectives due to previous mix-ups.

questions.question: Feeling 'a bit under the weather' means you feel:
questions.learningObjective: Understand everyday health idioms
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' is a common idiom that means you feel a little bit sick.
misconceptions: It sounds like weather, but it's an idiom about health.
You guessed 'very busy' before for a similar phrase, but this is about being sick.
It means you are unwell, the opposite of energetic.
questions.curriculumReason: Addressing a specific incorrect answer from the last round.

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'massive'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify the antonym for massive
questions.explanation: Massive means extremely big, so the opposite is small.
misconceptions: Heavy is about weight, not size.
Giant means the same thing as massive.
Fast is about speed, not size.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing missed antonyms.

questions.question: Who helps you check out a book at the library?
questions.learningObjective: Identify library personnel
questions.explanation: A librarian is the person who works at a library and helps you borrow books.
misconceptions: Doctors work in clinics or hospitals.
questions.curriculumReason: Spaced review of library topics.

questions.question: We always ___ breakfast together as a family.
questions.learningObjective: Use correct verb form for 'we' in habits
questions.explanation: With 'we' for a daily habit, just use the base verb 'eat'.
misconceptions: Add 's' only for he, she, or it.
The word 'always' shows a current routine, not the past.
questions.curriculumReason: Practice routine verbs.

questions.question: She is very good ___ solving math problems.
questions.learningObjective: Use 'good at' to describe skills
questions.explanation: When talking about a skill you do well, we say you are 'good at' it.
misconceptions: We do not use 'in' after 'good' for skills.
We do not use 'on' after 'good' for skills.
You can be 'good with tools', but for an activity use 'at'.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing collocations that were missed due to time.

questions.question: The missing letter ___ yesterday morning.
questions.learningObjective: Use past simple passive voice correctly
questions.explanation: Because the letter didn't do the action itself, we use the passive voice: 'was found'.
misconceptions: Use the past participle 'found', not the base verb 'find'.
The letter did not find something; it was found by someone.
The letter cannot find anything itself.
questions.curriculumReason: Spaced review for past simple passive.

questions.question: What does the word 'exhausted' mean?
questions.learningObjective: Define the word exhausted correctly
questions.explanation: Exhausted is a strong adjective that means you have zero energy left. You are very tired.
misconceptions: You mixed this up before! Exhausted means tired, not excited.
Confused means you do not understand something.
questions.curriculumReason: Directly addressing the misconception where the player chose 'very excited' instead of tired.

questions.question: If someone is sick but is 'on the mend', they are:
questions.learningObjective: Understand the meaning of 'on the mend'
questions.explanation: 'Mend' means to fix. If a sick person is on the mend, they are healing and getting better.
misconceptions: On the mend is a positive phrase, not negative.
It refers to healing, not just sleeping.
They might have already seen a doctor, but this focuses on healing.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing more health idioms to clarify confusion.

questions.question: I will 'touch base' with you next week. This means I will:
questions.learningObjective: Understand the conversation idiom 'touch base'
questions.explanation: To 'touch base' means to quickly talk to someone to share an update.
misconceptions: It sounds like baseball, but it's a conversation idiom.
It does not involve physical travel.
It means the exact opposite of ignoring someone.
questions.curriculumReason: Spaced review for conversation idioms.

questions.question: Everyone ___ excited for the concert tonight.
questions.learningObjective: Use singular verbs with everyone
questions.explanation: Even though 'everyone' refers to a lot of people, the word itself is treated as singular, so we use 'is'.
misconceptions: 'Everyone' sounds plural, but it takes a singular verb.
The verb 'be' needs to be conjugated.
'Were' is past tense, but the concert is tonight.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing indefinite pronouns after missing a question in the last session.

questions.question: If an outcome cannot be stopped, it is:
questions.learningObjective: Identify words that mean impossible to stop
questions.explanation: If you cannot avoid something, it is unavoidable. It must happen.
misconceptions: Unlikely means it probably will not happen.
Unexpected means it was a surprise.
Unusual means it is weird or rare.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing inevitability vocabulary missed due to timeout.

questions.question: A decision that is agreed upon by everyone is:
questions.learningObjective: Define unanimous correctly
questions.explanation: When every single person in a group agrees on something, the decision is unanimous.
misconceptions: A secret is hidden, not necessarily agreed on.
Speed does not mean everyone agreed.
Controversial means people argue about it.
questions.curriculumReason: Directly targeting the confusion between unanimous, kept secret, and decided quickly.

questions.question: These beautiful leather shoes ___ in Italy.
questions.learningObjective: Form the passive voice correctly in the past simple
questions.explanation: Since the shoes receive the action (they didn't build themselves), we use the passive voice: 'were made'.
misconceptions: 'Made' alone implies the shoes did the making.
The correct form needs the past participle 'made', not 'make'.
questions.curriculumReason: Review of the past simple passive.

questions.question: I have always been interested ___ learning French.
questions.learningObjective: Pair 'interested' with the correct preposition
questions.explanation: In English, the word 'interested' is almost always followed by the preposition 'in'.
misconceptions: 'About' sounds okay, but it is not the correct grammar pair.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing common preposition collocations.

questions.question: What do we call a general agreement among a group?
questions.learningObjective: Identify words related to group agreement
questions.explanation: A consensus is when a group of people reach an agreement together.
misconceptions: An argument is when people disagree.
A secret is something hidden, not an agreement.
Failure means it did not work out.
questions.curriculumReason: Strengthening advanced agreement vocabulary.

questions.question: Neither of the boys ___ to go to the museum.
questions.learningObjective: Match neither with a singular verb
questions.explanation: The word 'neither' focuses on one person at a time (not this one, not that one), so it takes the singular verb 'wants'.
misconceptions: Needs a helping verb to use 'wanting'.
'Neither' is singular, so it needs 'wants', not 'want'.
'Neither' takes a singular verb, not the plural 'are'.
questions.curriculumReason: Drilling difficult indefinite pronoun rules.

questions.question: If someone says rain is 'inevitable', they mean it is:
questions.learningObjective: Define the word inevitable
questions.explanation: Inevitable describes a situation that is absolutely going to happen and cannot be prevented.
misconceptions: Inevitable means the exact opposite of unlikely.
Because it is expected, it is not surprising.
It doesn't describe how strong the rain is, just that it will happen.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing inevitability vocabulary.

questions.question: Stop 'beating around the bush' and just tell me!
questions.learningObjective: Understand the meaning of 'beating around the bush'
questions.explanation: To 'beat around the bush' means to avoid talking about what is really important.
misconceptions: This is an idiom; it's not actually about a real bush.
It is about conversation, not physical running.
questions.curriculumReason: Adding deeper conversation idioms to the review.

questions.question: If feelings of respect between two people are 'mutual', they are:
questions.learningObjective: Understand the word mutual in contexts of agreement and shared feelings
questions.explanation: Mutual means something is felt or shared equally by two or more people.
misconceptions: Mutual has nothing to do with time or speed.
Mutual describes who feels it, not how weak it is.
questions.curriculumReason: Ensuring understanding of mutual/shared states.

questions.question: If the weather outside is 'freezing', it is:
questions.learningObjective: Recognize extreme adjectives for temperature
questions.explanation: Freezing is an extreme adjective that means it is dangerously or uncomfortably cold.
misconceptions: Freezing is much stronger than chilly.
It might be windy, but freezing specifically means cold.
It can be freezing without any snow.
questions.curriculumReason: Drilling extreme adjectives.

questions.question: Looking 'green around the gills' means someone is:
questions.learningObjective: Understand health idiom for looking sick
questions.explanation: This idiom describes someone who looks sick to their stomach or nauseous, as if their face is slightly green.
misconceptions: 'Green with envy' means jealous, but gills refers to sickness.
Green can mean money, but not in this phrase.
This is an idiom, not about actually swimming like a fish.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing challenging health idioms.

questions.question: The famous Mona Lisa painting ___ by Leonardo da Vinci.
questions.learningObjective: Use past passive for historical actions
questions.explanation: We use the past passive 'was painted' because the artwork was created by someone in the past.
misconceptions: Da Vinci lived long ago, so it needs to be past tense, not 'is'.
questions.curriculumReason: Using passive voice in more complex historical sentences.

questions.question: Either option ___ fine with me. I don't mind.
questions.learningObjective: Match either with singular verbs
questions.explanation: The word 'either' is singular because you are choosing just one of the options. So we use 'is'.
misconceptions: 'Either' looks at one choice at a time, so it takes a singular verb.
The verb 'be' needs to be conjugated to 'is'.
The sentence is in the present tense, not past.
questions.curriculumReason: Tackling tricky agreement rules with either/neither.

questions.question: The team practiced so hard, they are 'bound to' win.
questions.learningObjective: Understand 'bound to' as high probability
questions.explanation: If something is 'bound to' happen, it means it is very likely or almost certain to occur.
misconceptions: Bound to means it will happen, not that they will lose.
It is an idiom, not about ropes or tying.
It means it is much stronger than just a hope.
questions.curriculumReason: Strengthening modality terms.

feedback.headline: Keep it up! You are making great progress.
strengths: You perfectly matched verbs for conditional sentences.
You did great with health expressions and places like the library.
weaknesses: You mixed up some common describing words, like joyful and angry.
You had some trouble choosing the right greetings for doorways.
feedback.advice: A lot of your answers ran out of time. Move your character to the correct lane first, then punch to lock it in before the timer ends!

curriculum.title: Describing Words and Everyday Basics
curriculum.rationale: We are going to practice everyday vocabulary and review verb tenses you have not seen in a while to keep your memory sharp.

targetConcepts.reason: You mixed up words like joyful and angry, so we will practice these.
We need to practice how to use verbs when talking about 'he' or 'she'.
We are revisiting how to politely invite someone inside.
We are going to practice the tricky word order after negative words.
Let's review the exact words for feeling very tired and very hungry.

curriculum.sessionStrategy: We will mix easy vocabulary practice with a few trickier grammar challenges to build your confidence and help you answer faster.

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'hot'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify the opposite of hot.
questions.explanation: The opposite of hot is cold. Warm means slightly hot, not the opposite.
misconceptions: Chose a word that means slightly hot instead of the opposite.
Chose a word that means extremely hot instead of the opposite.
Confused a flavor with a temperature.
questions.curriculumReason: This reviews simple opposites for temperature.

questions.question: Which word means the same as 'joyful'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify a synonym for joyful.
questions.explanation: Joyful means full of joy, so it means the same as happy.
misconceptions: Confused a positive feeling with a negative feeling of anger.
Confused a positive feeling with a feeling of sadness.
Guessed a physical state instead of an emotion.
questions.curriculumReason: You mixed up joyful and angry before, so we are practicing this topic.

questions.question: What should you say when someone knocks on your door?
questions.learningObjective: Choose the polite phrase to invite someone inside.
questions.explanation: Saying 'Come in!' is a friendly way to invite a guest into your room.
misconceptions: Chose a rude phrase instead of a welcoming one.
Chose a phrase that tells someone not to enter.
Chose an unfriendly phrase to push someone away.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices polite everyday greetings when someone visits.

questions.question: Choose the right verb: "I ___ going to the store."
questions.learningObjective: Use the correct form of 'be' with the first-person pronoun.
questions.explanation: We always use 'am' when talking about ourselves with the word 'I'.
misconceptions: Used the plural verb instead of the first-person singular.
Used the third-person verb instead of the first-person singular.
Used the base form of the verb without matching it to the subject.
questions.curriculumReason: We are reviewing how to talk about yourself in the present tense.

questions.question: Pick the correct verb for 'he': "Every morning, he ___ to school."
questions.learningObjective: Conjugate regular verbs for third-person singular subjects.
questions.explanation: When using 'he', 'she', or 'it' in the present tense, we add '-es' to 'go'.
misconceptions: Forgot to add the ending for a third-person subject.
Used the 'ing' form without a helper verb.
Used the past participle incorrectly in the present tense.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices verb endings when talking about another person.

questions.question: Fill in the blank for this sentence: "I ___ very happy today."
questions.learningObjective: Use 'am' with 'I' in a simple present sentence.
questions.explanation: We use 'am' with 'I' to talk about our feelings right now.
misconceptions: Used the verb form for 'he' or 'she'.
Used the verb form for 'you' or 'we'.
Used a past tense form instead of a present tense form.
questions.curriculumReason: This helps you remember to match the subject 'I' with the right verb.

questions.question: Find the exact opposite of 'boiling'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the extreme antonym of boiling.
questions.explanation: Boiling means extremely hot, so its exact opposite is freezing, which means extremely cold.
misconceptions: Chose a mild temperature instead of an extreme opposite.
Chose a synonym instead of an antonym.
Chose a mild opposite instead of the extreme opposite.
questions.curriculumReason: We are practicing how to describe extreme temperatures.

questions.question: Which feeling word is a match for 'happy'?
questions.learningObjective: Recognize joyful as a synonym for happy.
questions.explanation: Joyful is a descriptive word that means you are feeling a lot of happiness.
misconceptions: Confused a happy feeling with a mad feeling.
Confused a happy feeling with feeling uninterested.
Confused a happy feeling with a sad or angry feeling.
questions.curriculumReason: This builds your vocabulary for describing positive emotions.

questions.question: How do you politely invite a guest inside?
questions.learningObjective: Use polite social language at a doorway.
questions.explanation: 'Please come in' is the standard polite way to welcome someone through your door.
misconceptions: Chose an awkward command instead of a welcome.
Chose a direct rejection instead of a welcome.
Chose a warning sign phrase instead of a welcome.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices what to say when greeting people at your home.

questions.question: Select the right form: "She always ___ her homework."
questions.learningObjective: Apply the -es suffix to verbs ending in -sh for third-person singular.
questions.explanation: For 'she' in the present tense, we must add '-es' to the verb finish.
misconceptions: Forgot to change the verb for the subject 'she'.
Used an incomplete progressive form instead of simple present.
Used past tense instead of simple present for a routine.
questions.curriculumReason: This helps you correctly add endings to verbs for daily routines.

questions.question: Which phrase means 'exhausted'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify 'very tired' as the meaning of exhausted.
questions.explanation: When you are exhausted, it means you have no energy and are very tired.
misconceptions: Confused feeling tired with needing food.
Confused feeling tired with needing a drink.
questions.curriculumReason: We are practicing exact words to say how you feel physically.

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'abundant'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify rare as the antonym of abundant.
questions.explanation: Abundant means there is a lot of something. The opposite is rare, meaning it is hard to find.
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an antonym.
Chose a related quantity word instead of the opposite.
questions.curriculumReason: This reviews vocabulary for talking about amounts and quantities.

questions.question: What does it mean to feel 'under the weather'?
questions.learningObjective: Understand the idiom 'under the weather'.
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' is a common phrase that means you are feeling a little sick.
misconceptions: Chose the opposite of the idiom's meaning.
Confused a sickness idiom with a strength phrase.
Confused a physical feeling with an emotional one.
questions.curriculumReason: We are reviewing common phrases used to describe your health.

questions.question: Which word describes someone who is 'starving'?
questions.learningObjective: Define starving as very hungry.
questions.explanation: Starving is a strong word that means you need food and are very hungry.
misconceptions: Confused the need for food with the need for water.
Confused the need for food with a lack of sleep.
questions.curriculumReason: You previously mixed up words for tired and hungry, so we are practicing them.

questions.question: Complete this routine action: "The dog ___ loudly at strangers."
questions.learningObjective: Conjugate verbs for an animal (third-person singular).
questions.explanation: The subject 'the dog' acts like 'it', so we must add an 's' to the verb in the present tense.
misconceptions: Forgot to add the 's' for a singular noun.
Used the 'ing' form without a helper verb.
Used the past tense instead of the simple present for a routine.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices using the right verb forms for animals and objects.

questions.question: Find the opposite meaning for 'plentiful'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify scarce as the antonym of plentiful.
questions.explanation: Plentiful means there is plenty to go around. Scarce is the opposite, meaning there is very little.
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an opposite.
Chose a word meaning sufficient rather than the opposite.
Chose a word meaning a surplus instead of a shortage.
questions.curriculumReason: This builds your vocabulary for describing when there is not enough of something.

questions.question: What is another way to say 'glad'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify pleased as a synonym for glad.
questions.explanation: Glad and pleased both mean you are happy about a situation.
misconceptions: Chose a negative feeling instead of a positive one.
Chose a word for sadness or anger instead of happiness.
Chose a word indicating a lack of understanding.
questions.curriculumReason: We are expanding your list of words to describe positive emotions.

questions.question: If someone is 'on the mend', how are they feeling?
questions.learningObjective: Understand the meaning of the idiom 'on the mend'.
questions.explanation: 'On the mend' means that your health is mending, or getting better after being sick.
misconceptions: Chose becoming ill instead of recovering.
Chose declining health instead of improving health.
Chose an action related to being sick rather than the feeling of recovery.
questions.curriculumReason: This helps you talk about getting better after an illness.

questions.question: What is the best meaning for 'furious'?
questions.learningObjective: Define furious as very angry.
questions.explanation: Furious is a strong descriptive word that means you are very angry.
questions.curriculumReason: We are practicing words that express very strong emotions.

questions.question: Which phrase welcomes someone who just arrived?
questions.learningObjective: Select the correct greeting for an arrival.
questions.explanation: 'Welcome' is the right word to greet someone arriving. The other choices are used when someone is leaving.
misconceptions: Used a departing phrase instead of a welcoming one.
Used a phrase for leaving instead of arriving.
Used a phrase for travel rather than welcoming a guest.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices basic social phrases for hosting guests.

questions.question: Pick the correct word order: "Never before ___ such a beautiful sunset."
questions.learningObjective: Apply subject-auxiliary inversion after a negative adverbial phrase.
questions.explanation: After phrases like 'Never before', we flip the subject and the helper verb, so 'I have' becomes 'have I'.
misconceptions: Kept standard word order after a negative adverbial.
Used 'did' with a past tense verb incorrectly.
Used standard past tense without inversion.
questions.curriculumReason: We are practicing the tricky rule of flipping words after negative phrases.

questions.question: Which word means something cannot be stopped from happening?
questions.learningObjective: Understand unavoidable as inevitably occurring.
questions.explanation: If a situation cannot be stopped, it is unavoidable. The 'un-' means not.
misconceptions: Chose a word meaning the opposite.
Chose a word meaning you have a choice.
Chose a word meaning it can be stopped.
questions.curriculumReason: This helps you describe things that are certain to happen.

questions.question: Complete this sentence: "Rarely ___ this late."
questions.learningObjective: Invert subject and auxiliary verb after 'rarely'.
questions.explanation: When starting a sentence with a negative word like 'Rarely', we swap the normal order to sound like a question.
misconceptions: Used standard word order without inversion.
Added 'does' but failed to invert it with the subject.
Used the 'be' verb instead of 'do' for an action verb.
questions.curriculumReason: We are practicing advanced word order when sentences begin with negative words.

questions.question: What describes an event that can be prevented?
questions.learningObjective: Define avoidable as something that can be prevented.
questions.explanation: If you can prevent it or avoid it, it is avoidable.
misconceptions: Chose a word meaning it cannot be stopped.
Chose the exact opposite of preventable.
Chose a word meaning it is definitely going to happen.
questions.curriculumReason: This reviews vocabulary about whether events can be changed or not.

questions.question: Fill the gap: "Not only ___ the game, but they also broke the record."
questions.learningObjective: Use inversion after 'Not only'.
questions.explanation: Starting a sentence with 'Not only' forces us to use question word order, like 'did they win'.
misconceptions: Used standard statement word order instead of inverted.
Added an auxiliary verb but failed to invert it.
Inverted the main verb directly without an auxiliary.
questions.curriculumReason: This practices the special grammar rule used with the phrase 'Not only'.

questions.learningObjective: Pair the adjective 'responsible' with the correct preposition
questions.explanation: When you are in charge of something, you are 'responsible for' it.
misconceptions: Used 'to', which pairs with verbs or directions.
questions.curriculumReason: Preposition combinations are tricky and need regular review.

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'Excessive'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for extreme quantity adjectives
questions.explanation: 'Excessive' means too much. Its opposite is 'inadequate', meaning not enough.
misconceptions: Chose a synonym meaning a lot of something.
Chose a synonym for having enough.
Chose a word describing physical size instead of quantity.
questions.curriculumReason: A final tough challenge on quantity antonyms.

curriculum.title: Everyday Words and Timing
curriculum.rationale: You showed great skill with hard grammar rules, but slipped up on a few everyday phrases and basic opposites. We will brush up on those while reviewing a few older topics.

targetConcepts.reason: You recently picked a command to sit instead of a friendly welcome.

curriculum.sessionStrategy: Focus on everyday vocabulary and common grammar mix-ups using mostly familiar words, while occasionally challenging you to remember older spelling and grammar rules.

questions.question: Which of these words is a colour?
questions.learningObjective: Identify basic colour vocabulary.
questions.explanation: "Purple" is a colour. Words like "chair" are physical objects, not colours!
misconceptions: Chose a noun instead of a colour
Chose an adverb instead of a colour
Chose a conjunction instead of a colour
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing basic word classes due to a recent mistake.

questions.question: What is the exact opposite of the word 'big'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for size adjectives.
questions.explanation: "Small" is the opposite of "big". "Tall" means high, which is actually similar to big!
misconceptions: Chose a dimension instead of the opposite
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting the specific misconception of confusing 'tall' and 'small'.

questions.question: What do you say to welcome someone who knocks on your door?
questions.learningObjective: Use appropriate social language at a doorway.
questions.explanation: You say "Come in!" to invite someone inside. "Sit down!" is what you say after they are already inside the room.
misconceptions: Chose a rejection instead of a welcome
Chose a command to sit instead of enter
Chose a posture command instead of enter
questions.curriculumReason: Addressing the recent error of saying 'Sit down' at the door.

questions.question: Where do you go to borrow a book to read?
questions.learningObjective: Identify everyday places and their functions.
questions.explanation: A "library" is where you borrow books. A "market" is where you buy food and goods!
misconceptions: Chose a place to buy food
questions.curriculumReason: Correcting the recent confusion between a market and a library.

questions.question: What is the opposite of a 'generous' and giving person?
questions.learningObjective: Identify personality adjective antonyms.
questions.explanation: "Selfish" people keep things for themselves, which is the exact opposite of generous. "Kind" means nice, which is similar to generous!
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
questions.curriculumReason: You recently chose 'Kind' instead of 'Selfish'.

questions.question: Which verb fits this sentence: 'I ___ very tired today.'?
questions.learningObjective: Use the correct form of the verb 'to be' for first person.
questions.explanation: With "I", we always use "am". "Is" goes with he/she/it, and "are" goes with you/we/they.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing foundational grammar concepts to ensure mastery.

questions.question: What is a polite way to greet your teacher at 8 AM?
questions.learningObjective: Use appropriate morning greetings.
questions.explanation: At 8 AM, it is the morning, so you say "Good morning".
misconceptions: Chose a farewell instead of a greeting
questions.curriculumReason: Strengthening your mastery of everyday greetings.

questions.question: Identify the word that describes a dark shade used in painting.
questions.learningObjective: Identify basic colour vocabulary.
questions.explanation: "Black" is a colour. A "table" is a piece of furniture!
misconceptions: Chose an object instead of a colour
Chose an action instead of a colour
Chose a sound instead of a colour
questions.curriculumReason: Extra practice for basic word classes based on recent misses.

questions.question: Which word means the opposite of 'huge' in size?
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for size adjectives.
questions.explanation: "Tiny" means very small, which is the exact opposite of "huge". "Enormous" means the same as huge!
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
Chose a volume instead of size
Chose a weight instead of size
questions.curriculumReason: More practice finding the opposite of size words.

questions.question: Where would you typically go to buy a fresh loaf of bread?
questions.learningObjective: Identify shops and what they sell.
questions.explanation: A "bakery" bakes and sells bread. A library is for books, not bread!
questions.curriculumReason: Building on your success with everyday places.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'break the ice' mean when meeting people?
questions.learningObjective: Understand common conversation idioms.
questions.explanation: To "break the ice" means to start a conversation and make people feel relaxed. It has nothing to do with cancelling plans!
questions.curriculumReason: You recently mistook 'cancel a plan' for a conversation idiom.

questions.question: Which preposition correctly completes: 'She is interested ___ art.'?
questions.learningObjective: Use correct adjective-preposition collocations.
questions.explanation: We always say "interested in" something. "Interested on" is not used in English!
questions.curriculumReason: Addressing the specific mix-up of using 'on' instead of 'in'.

questions.question: Complete the routine sentence: 'We usually ___ tennis on Fridays.'
questions.learningObjective: Use the present simple for first-person plural routines.
questions.explanation: For habits and routines with "we", use the base verb "play". "Playing" needs an 'are' and means it is happening right now!
questions.curriculumReason: You chose 'playing' for a routine action recently.

questions.question: What is the opposite of having an 'abundant' amount?
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for quantity adjectives.
questions.explanation: "Scarce" means there is very little of something, which is the exact opposite of "abundant" (having plenty).
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing quantity antonyms which have been tricky lately.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelled word that means to get something.
questions.learningObjective: Correctly spell words with 'ie' and 'ei'.
questions.explanation: The rule is "i before e, except after c". Since there is a "c", it is spelled "receive".
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting the 'ie/ei' spelling rule due to a recent miss.

questions.question: What does it mean when someone says they feel 'under the weather'?
questions.learningObjective: Understand common health idioms.
questions.explanation: Feeling "under the weather" is a common phrase that means you feel a little sick.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing health idioms to reinforce your knowledge.

questions.question: Complete the history fact: 'The letter ___ yesterday.'
questions.learningObjective: Use the past simple passive voice.
questions.explanation: The letter didn't write itself, so we need the passive voice "was written" to show what happened to it yesterday.
questions.curriculumReason: Working on passive forms for past events.

questions.question: Which word has a similar meaning to feeling 'cheerful'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify synonyms for common adjectives.
questions.explanation: "Joyful" and "cheerful" both mean feeling very happy.
questions.curriculumReason: Reinforcing your strong grasp of common synonyms.

questions.question: If you 'catch up' with a friend over coffee, what are you doing?
questions.learningObjective: Understand conversational phrasal verbs.
questions.explanation: To "catch up" means to talk to someone you haven't seen in a while and share your latest news.
questions.curriculumReason: Continuing practice with conversation phrases.

questions.question: Fill in the blank for this skill: 'He is good ___ playing the guitar.'
questions.learningObjective: Use correct adjective-preposition collocations.
questions.explanation: In English, you are "good at" a skill. We do not say "good in" or "good on"!
questions.curriculumReason: Further practice with tricky prepositions after adjectives.

questions.question: How do you correctly finish the conditional: 'If it rains tomorrow, I ___ at home.'?
questions.learningObjective: Use the first conditional to express future possibilities.
questions.explanation: For real future possibilities, use "If + present, will + verb". So, "If it rains, I will stay."
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting the first conditional structure which needs review.

questions.question: Which phrase completes the hypothetical statement: 'Were I you, I ___ that car.'?
questions.learningObjective: Use inverted second conditional forms.
questions.explanation: "Were I you" is a formal way to say "If I were you". It requires "would" in the second part: "I would buy".
questions.curriculumReason: Maintaining your skills with advanced conditionals.

questions.question: Complete the dramatic opening: 'Never before ___ seen such a beautiful sunset.'
questions.learningObjective: Use negative adverbial inversion correctly.
questions.explanation: When a sentence starts with a negative word like "Never", the subject and verb trade places. So it becomes "have I".
misconceptions: Forgot to invert subject and verb
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing advanced sentence structures you have shown strength in.

questions.question: What does the adjective 'unanimous' mean in a group decision context?
questions.learningObjective: Understand advanced vocabulary related to agreement.
questions.explanation: "Unanimous" means everyone in the group fully agrees on the decision.
questions.curriculumReason: Reinforcing your knowledge of advanced vocabulary.

questions.question: Which word describes a situation that is certain to happen?
questions.learningObjective: Understand vocabulary related to modality and inevitability.
questions.explanation: "Unavoidable" means you cannot avoid it; it is absolutely going to happen.
misconceptions: Chose a word meaning no chance
Chose a word meaning low chance
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing high-level inevitability vocabulary.

questions.question: What is a formal academic synonym for a 'difficult' task?
questions.learningObjective: Identify academic synonyms for common adjectives.
questions.explanation: "Arduous" is a formal word meaning very difficult and requiring a lot of effort. "Gentle" means soft or mild!
questions.curriculumReason: You recently chose 'Gentle' instead of a synonym for hard or difficult.

questions.question: Complete this past regret clause: 'Had I known the truth, I ___ helped you.'
questions.learningObjective: Use third conditional inversion.
questions.explanation: "Had I known" means "If I had known". The second part must be "would have" plus the past participle to talk about the past.
questions.curriculumReason: Solidifying your grasp on inverted past conditionals.

questions.question: Which structure fits the prediction: 'If she studies hard, she ___ the exam.'?
questions.learningObjective: Use the first conditional to make predictions.
questions.explanation: For a real future condition, we use "will" in the result clause: "she will pass".
questions.curriculumReason: Extra practice on the first conditional structure.

questions.question: What is a formal verb that means to 'look into' an issue?
questions.learningObjective: Identify formal verb synonyms.
questions.explanation: "Investigate" is a formal way to say you are going to look into or study an issue closely.
misconceptions: Chose an action meaning to not look
Chose an action meaning to lose memory
Chose an action meaning to conceal
questions.curriculumReason: Expanding your advanced synonym vocabulary.

questions.question: Choose the right form for this past event: 'The famous bridge ___ in 1999.'
questions.learningObjective: Use the past simple passive for historical facts.
questions.explanation: A bridge doesn't build itself! We use "was built" to show that someone built it in the past.
questions.curriculumReason: Strengthening your use of passive voice in the past tense.

feedback.headline: Great energy, but let's sync up your timing!

You correctly answered polite greetings and doorway phrases.

weaknesses: You often mix up prepositions, like saying 'interested on' instead of 'interested in'.
You struggled with first conditional sentences, using 'were' instead of 'will'.
You got confused on some synonyms and antonyms, like matching 'huge' instead of 'small'.

curriculum.title: Finding the Right Rhythm and Words

questions.question: Which word describes the color of a banana?
questions.learningObjective: Identify basic color vocabulary.
questions.explanation: 'Yellow' is a color. 'Apple' and 'Car' are things, and 'Quickly' describes how you do something.
misconceptions: Chose a fruit instead of a color
Chose a noun instead of a color
Chose an adverb instead of a color
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting weak basic word class performance.

questions.question: Identify the color word for a clear daytime sky.
questions.learningObjective: Identify basic color vocabulary.
questions.explanation: The sky is 'Blue' on a clear day. 'Cloud' and 'Rain' are things in the sky, not colors.
misconceptions: Chose a thing in the sky, not a color
Chose weather instead of a color
Chose a shade, not the actual color of the sky
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing basic vocabulary foundations.

questions.question: Find the exact opposite of the word 'large'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for size adjectives.
questions.explanation: The opposite of 'large' is 'small'. Words like 'huge' and 'giant' mean the same thing as large!
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
Chose a related dimension instead of the exact opposite
Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
questions.curriculumReason: Addressing the specific mistake of choosing 'Huge' instead of 'Small'.

questions.question: Choose the word that means the opposite of 'tiny'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for size adjectives.
questions.explanation: 'Huge' is the opposite of 'tiny'. 'Tiny' means very small, so the opposite must be very big.
misconceptions: Chose a word for time instead of size
Chose an opinion instead of size
Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing size antonyms to clear up recent confusion.

questions.question: We usually ___ football on Saturdays.
questions.learningObjective: Use correct present simple verb forms for first-person plural.
questions.explanation: For routines with 'we', use the base verb 'play'. 'Playing' needs an 'are' before it, like 'we are playing'.
misconceptions: Used the 'ing' form without a 'be' verb
Added an 's' which is only for he/she/it
Used past tense for a routine action

questions.question: Complete this sentence: Every morning, we ___ breakfast together.
questions.learningObjective: Use correct present simple verb forms for first-person plural.
questions.explanation: When talking about a habit using 'we', just use the base verb 'eat'.
misconceptions: Used 'ing' form without a helping verb
Added an 's' which is only for singular subjects
Used past tense for a daily habit
questions.curriculumReason: Reinforcing present simple verbs after a recent error.

questions.question: Where would you go to buy fresh bread?
questions.learningObjective: Identify everyday shopping locations.
questions.explanation: A bakery is where fresh bread and cakes are made and sold. A garage is for cars.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing after choosing 'Garage' instead of 'Bakery'.

questions.question: Select the place where you can purchase medicine.
questions.learningObjective: Identify everyday shopping locations.
questions.explanation: A pharmacy is the shop where you buy medicine.
questions.curriculumReason: Further practice on everyday locations.

questions.question: What should you say when someone knocks on your office door?
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate social responses for entering rooms.
questions.explanation: When someone knocks, 'Come in!' is the polite way to tell them they can enter.
questions.curriculumReason: Building on your strength with doorway language.

questions.question: How do you politely ask to enter a room?
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate social questions for entering rooms.
questions.explanation: 'May I come in?' is the most polite way to ask if you can enter a room.
misconceptions: Chose a question about their location
questions.curriculumReason: Building on your strength with doorway language.

questions.question: He always ___ his keys on the kitchen counter.
questions.learningObjective: Apply third-person singular rules in present simple.
questions.explanation: For a routine action with 'he', 'she', or 'it', we add an 's' to the verb, making it 'leaves'.
misconceptions: Forgot to add 's' for a third-person subject
Used present continuous for a habit
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting low performance on third-person verbs.

questions.question: Select the correct verb: She ___ to the gym after work.
questions.learningObjective: Apply third-person singular rules in present simple.
questions.explanation: Because the subject is 'she' and it is a routine, the verb needs an 'es' at the end: 'goes'.
misconceptions: Forgot the 'es' for a third-person subject
Used past participle instead of present verb
questions.curriculumReason: Providing more repetition for tricky verb endings.

questions.question: Pick the antonym for someone who is 'generous'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for personality traits.
questions.explanation: Someone who is generous loves to share. The opposite is 'selfish', someone who keeps things for themselves.
misconceptions: Chose a synonym instead of an antonym
Chose a trait about money, not giving
questions.curriculumReason: Correcting the mistake of choosing 'Cheerful' instead of 'Selfish'.

questions.question: What is the opposite of a 'cheerful' person?
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for personality traits.
questions.explanation: A cheerful person is happy and positive. The opposite is 'grumpy', meaning bad-tempered.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing more personality opposites.

questions.question: Find the opposite meaning of 'abundant'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify antonyms for quantity adjectives.
questions.explanation: 'Abundant' means there is a lot of something. The opposite is 'scarce', which means there is very little.
misconceptions: Chose a size word instead of a quantity word
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing a missed antonym question from the last session.

questions.question: What does it mean to feel 'under the weather'?
questions.learningObjective: Understand common health-related idioms.
questions.explanation: Feeling 'under the weather' is an idiom that means you feel a little sick.
questions.curriculumReason: You missed a health idiom question recently, so we are reviewing this topic.

questions.question: If someone is 'fit as a fiddle', they are...
questions.learningObjective: Understand common health-related idioms.
questions.explanation: If you are 'fit as a fiddle', you are in excellent health and physical condition!
misconceptions: Took 'fiddle' literally as a musical instrument
questions.curriculumReason: More practice with health idioms to build your confidence.

questions.question: The letter ___ by the manager yesterday.
questions.learningObjective: Form past simple passive sentences.
questions.explanation: Since it happened 'yesterday', we use the past passive 'was read'.
questions.curriculumReason: You did great on this topic, so here is a quick review.

questions.question: Which passive verb fits: The cake ___ by my sister.
questions.learningObjective: Form past simple passive sentences.
questions.explanation: The cake didn't bake itself! It 'was baked' by someone. This is the past passive form.
questions.curriculumReason: Another review of your strength with passive voice.

questions.question: What is another way to say you are 'exhausted'?
questions.learningObjective: Understand intense vocabulary words.
questions.explanation: When you are 'exhausted', you have zero energy left. It means 'very tired'.
questions.curriculumReason: Clarifying intense vocabulary after selecting 'Very excited' for 'Very tired'.

questions.question: She is very interested ___ learning new languages.
questions.learningObjective: Pair adjectives with correct prepositions.
questions.explanation: In English, we always say we are interested 'in' something, never interested 'on' or 'at'.
questions.curriculumReason: Fixing a repeated mistake with prepositions following adjectives.

questions.question: He is quite good ___ playing the piano.
questions.learningObjective: Pair adjectives with correct prepositions.
questions.explanation: When you have a skill, you are good 'at' it. For example, good 'at' math or good 'at' playing piano.
questions.curriculumReason: More practice pairing adjectives with tricky little prepositions.

questions.question: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ stay home.
questions.learningObjective: Form first conditional sentences correctly.
questions.explanation: In a first conditional sentence (If + present), the main part uses 'will' to show a future result.
misconceptions: Used present continuous instead of future
questions.curriculumReason: Working on conditionals after you incorrectly chose 'were'.

questions.question: Fill in the conditional blank: If you study hard, you ___ pass the exam.
questions.learningObjective: Form first conditional sentences correctly.
questions.explanation: 'If you study hard' is a real possibility, so we use 'will' for the result: 'you will pass'.
questions.curriculumReason: Reinforcing the 'will' future result for realistic conditionals.

questions.question: Which word is a synonym for 'complex'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify synonyms for academic adjectives.
questions.explanation: Something that is 'complex' has many parts and is difficult to understand, so 'hard' is a good synonym.
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting the mistake of confusing 'Simple' and 'Hard'.

questions.question: Find a synonym that matches 'crucial'.
questions.learningObjective: Identify synonyms for academic adjectives.
questions.explanation: If something is 'crucial', it is absolutely necessary or 'important'.
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing more challenging academic adjectives.

questions.question: What is a good synonym for 'meticulous'?
questions.learningObjective: Identify synonyms for advanced adjectives.
questions.explanation: A 'meticulous' person pays close attention to detail, so 'thorough' is the matching synonym. It is the opposite of 'careless'.
questions.curriculumReason: Correcting a recent mistake where you chose 'Careless' instead of 'Thorough'.

questions.question: Choose the formal synonym for 'begin'.
questions.learningObjective: Match formal verbs with their simpler synonyms.
questions.explanation: 'Commence' is a formal, professional way to say 'begin' or 'start'.
misconceptions: Chose a word meaning to put off
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing formal verbs after confusing 'Delay' and 'Commence'.

questions.question: Which formal verb means to 'put off' a meeting?
questions.learningObjective: Match formal verbs with their simpler meanings.
questions.explanation: To 'postpone' a meeting means to push it to a later time, or 'put it off'.
questions.curriculumReason: Expanding your formal business vocabulary.

questions.question: Which word means that something is certain to happen?
questions.learningObjective: Understand vocabulary expressing certainty.
questions.explanation: If something is 'inevitable', it is absolutely going to happen and cannot be stopped.
misconceptions: Chose a word meaning it cannot happen
Chose a word meaning probably not
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing certainty vocabulary that you handled well in the past.

questions.question: What do you say when someone knocks on your door?

misconceptions: Chose Sit down! instead of Come in!
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting repeated mistakes with welcoming phrases at the door.

questions.question: Which phrase is a morning greeting for your family?
questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct phrase used to greet someone in the morning.
questions.explanation: In the early part of the day, we say 'Good morning'. 'Goodbye' is only for when you are leaving.
misconceptions: Chose Goodbye instead of Good morning
questions.curriculumReason: Targeting the mistake of saying goodbye instead of good morning.

questions.question: Choose the correct verb for yourself: I ___ very happy today.
questions.learningObjective: Use the correct present tense form of 'to be' for the first person.
questions.explanation: When you talk about yourself using 'I', the correct matching word is 'am'. We use 'is' for he, she, or it.
misconceptions: Used base form instead of conjugated verb
questions.curriculumReason: Correcting the use of 'is' instead of 'am' for the first person.

questions.question: Select the word that describes a color.
questions.learningObjective: Identify colors among other basic word classes.
questions.explanation: 'Blue' is a color you can see, like the sky. The other words are things or actions.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing a concept that is due for spaced practice.

questions.question: Pick the exact opposite of the word huge.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the antonym of the word 'huge'.
questions.explanation: 'Small' is the exact opposite of huge. 'Giant' means the same thing as huge!
questions.curriculumReason: Addressing the confusion between words for very large and very small.

questions.question: How do we say that we play soccer every weekend?
questions.learningObjective: Use the correct present simple verb form for 'we'.
questions.explanation: When we talk about 'we', the action word stays simple as 'play'. We only add an 's' for he, she, or it.
misconceptions: Added third-person s to first-person plural
questions.curriculumReason: Practicing a missed question regarding first-person plural verbs.

questions.question: Identify the shop where you buy fresh bread.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the purpose of a bakery.
questions.explanation: A bakery is a special shop that makes and sells bread and cakes. A bank is for money.
misconceptions: Confused money place with food place
Confused book place with food place
questions.curriculumReason: Reinforcing a strength in identifying everyday shopping places.

questions.question: Find the word that means the opposite of hot.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the antonym of the word 'hot'.
questions.explanation: 'Cold' is the opposite of hot. 'Warm' is only a little bit hot, not the full opposite.
questions.curriculumReason: Reviewing a strength to build confidence with opposites.

questions.question: He ___ to the store every day to buy milk.
questions.learningObjective: Use the correct present simple verb form for the third person.
questions.explanation: When talking about he, she, or it, we usually add an 's' or 'es' to the action. So 'go' becomes 'goes'.
questions.curriculumReason: Fixing the missing 's' on verbs for the third person.

questions.question: Which of these choices is a bright color?
questions.learningObjective: Identify colors among other basic word classes.
questions.explanation: 'Yellow' is a bright color, like the sun. The others are objects or feelings.
misconceptions: Chose a noun instead of a color
Chose a verb instead of a color
Chose an emotion instead of a color
questions.curriculumReason: Extra practice on an older topic due for review.

questions.question: A friend arrives at your house. You open the front door and say:
